paragraphs.heading: What it says
paragraphs.text: The law of large numbers says that if you take many independent random samples, the average of the results settles toward the true value, provided one exists. Stated more formally, for values that are independent and identically distributed, the sample mean converges to the true mean. It guarantees stable long-run results for the averages of some random events. Today it is used in statistics, probability theory, economics, insurance and other fields.

paragraphs.heading: Dice and coins
paragraphs.text: Roll a large number of six-sided dice and the average of their values, called the sample mean, gets close to 3.5, and closer still as more dice are rolled. A fair coin works the same way. One flip comes up heads with probability 1⁄2, so over a large number of flips the share of heads should be roughly 1⁄2. As the number of flips heads toward infinity, that share almost surely converges to 1⁄2.

paragraphs.heading: The gap still grows
paragraphs.text: There is a twist. The share of heads approaches 1⁄2, yet the plain difference between the number of heads and the number of tails almost surely becomes large as the flips pile up. That difference grows, but more slowly than the number of flips. So the difference divided by the number of flips still shrinks toward zero.

paragraphs.heading: Only for large numbers
paragraphs.text: The law applies only when many observations are considered. A handful of results need not match the expected value, and a streak of one outcome is not promptly balanced out by the others; expecting that is the gambler's fallacy. A casino may lose money on one spin of roulette, but over many spins its earnings move toward a predictable percentage, and any winning streak a player has is eventually overcome by the game. More trials also cannot cure a selection bias built into the trials: the bias stays.

paragraphs.heading: Computing by chance
paragraphs.text: Monte Carlo methods are another example of the law at work. They are a broad family of computer algorithms that reach numerical results through repeated random sampling. The more repetitions, the better the approximation tends to be. They matter mainly because other approaches are sometimes hard or impossible to use.

paragraphs.heading: When averages do not settle
paragraphs.text: In some cases the average does not converge at all. Take results drawn from a Cauchy distribution, or from certain Pareto distributions (α<1): the average of n results does not settle down as n grows, because their tails are heavy. The Cauchy distribution has no expected value, while the Pareto one (α<1) has an infinite expected value. For the Cauchy case, the average of n results has the same distribution as a single result.

paragraphs.heading: From Cardano to Khinchin
paragraphs.text: Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576) stated, without proof, that empirical statistics grow more accurate as trials increase. Jacob Bernoulli first proved a special form, for a binary random variable, after more than 20 years of work, and published it in his Ars Conjectandi in 1713. He called it his golden theorem, but it became known as Bernoulli's theorem, and Poisson later described it as the law of large numbers. Chebyshev, Markov, Borel, Cantelli, Kolmogorov and Khinchin refined it further, leading to a weak law and a strong law, where the strong form implies the weak.
